messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

David, a 56-year-old European American musician, came for help after years of feeling as though his world had narrowed to a few “safe” rooms and routines. He had been married for decades, and his wife had increasingly noticed how carefully he arranged his days around places he trusted: the home studio, the kitchen table early in the morning, the back porch at dusk. Outside those small islands, he felt on guard. Sudden movements from other people could put him immediately on edge, and if he was in a crowd or anywhere he associated with authority—security staff, police, uniformed personnel—his body tightened before he could think. He described an irritable, snappish temper that had grown harder to hide, though he was ashamed of it and tried to keep it contained. What frightened him most was that he no longer felt able to move through ordinary life without scanning for danger, as if safety existed only in a very limited number of places.

The assault that changed him had happened after a late-night performance nearly a year earlier. David had been leaving a small venue when a man he knew from the local music scene—someone he had once socialized with at clubs and after gigs—cornered him in a back hallway. David remembered the smell of a sharp, expensive cologne first, then the hard jolt of being shoved against the wall. There was violence, a crushing sense of powerlessness, and blood when he bit his lip trying to fight free. The rest of the event is not something he can tell in a clear sequence, even to himself. He remembers some moments with painful clarity: the cologne, the glint of a ring, the pressure of a hand, the taste of blood. Other parts are blank. When he tries to put it into words, he finds himself pushing the memory away before he can fully recall it, because the fragments come with such force that he feels he will be overwhelmed if he lets them gather into a whole story.

Since then, the brokenness of the memory has itself become part of what unsettles him. The more he tries to hold it at bay, the more it returns in pieces, and the more his mind seems to fill in gaps with alarm. He has come to fear that if he allowed himself to remember too much, he would be flooded by rage, shame, or panic. In response, he has made a rule for himself never to allow himself to feel or express anger. That rule has helped him stay functional in the short term, but it has also left him feeling tense and bottled up, as if any sign of anger would make him dangerous or exposed. He notices that this same guardedness now shapes what he avoids: he stays away from people in authority or uniform, because their presence feels too much like the helplessness of that night, and he avoids seeing people he socialized with before the event, especially anyone from the music circuit who might remind him of the attacker or ask questions he cannot answer.

Specific reminders now seem to reach him through the body before reason has time to intervene. Violence in movies, arguments in public, or even a raised voice can put him instantly on guard, because his mind links any sign of aggression with what happened in that hallway. Blood is another sharp trigger; the smallest sight of it can pull him back toward the assault and make him feel that something terrible is about to happen again. The cologne is the most unsettling of all. If a stranger passes too close in a store or backstage at a show wearing a similar scent, his chest tightens and he becomes hyperalert, scanning the room for exits and for the nearest person who might move abruptly. In those moments, his careful avoidance does not feel voluntary so much as necessary: he has learned that keeping distance from those reminders is the only way to keep himself steady.

Yet that same narrowing of his life has fed the problem. Because he is constantly restricting where he goes and who he sees, the memory never gets a chance to settle into any coherent shape, and each fragment remains charged and unfinished. The more he suppresses anger and keeps to himself, the less he can sort through what happened, and the less ordered the memory becomes. In turn, the unfinished pieces keep his sense of threat alive, so that a smell, a splash of blood, or a sudden movement can still feel as if it belongs to the assault. David finally sought therapy after his wife told him that his vigilance, irritability, and shrinking world were becoming impossible to ignore, and after he realized he had turned down performances simply to avoid venues where he might encounter old acquaintances or anyone in a uniform. He is hoping to regain a wider life and to stop living as though danger waits in every doorway, though he is most afraid that if he lets the memory in, he will lose control of the anger he has spent years trying not to feel.
